opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is a story I tell fairly often, because it was a real turning point for me. Before around 2017, I held what I'd now call a fairly optimistic, almost Platonic view: that intelligence and wisdom were deeply entangled. The intuition was that if you built a system that was genuinely, generally capable, one that could model the world richly, understand other agents, reason about consequences, then it would almost inevitably converge on something like good values. Understanding the world deeply enough would show you why cooperation and care make sense. In a sense I was betting against the orthogonality thesis.

AlphaGo was impressive, but you could still say it bootstrapped from human games, so maybe it absorbed some human sensibility along the way. AlphaGo Zero removed that crutch. It started from nothing but the rules and self-play, and within days it was superhuman, far beyond anything humanity had built up over thousands of years of studying Go. What struck me was that this capability came from pure optimization against an objective. There was no point where it needed to become wise, or reflective about whether winning at Go was worth doing. It just got extraordinarily good at the thing it was pointed at.

That made the orthogonality picture feel concrete rather than theoretical. You can scale competence in a domain enormously through search and self-play without anything resembling judgment about ends emerging alongside it. And if that pattern generalizes, if the path to very powerful systems runs through optimizing objectives in rich environments, then capability and wisdom come apart. Wisdom isn't a free byproduct; it has to be engineered in, or you have to constrain what the system is allowed to do.

That's a big part of why I shifted toward safety work, and eventually toward the approach I've been pursuing: rather than hoping a powerful system turns out wise, build frameworks where we can specify what's acceptable, model the relevant parts of the world explicitly, and get verifiable guarantees about behavior. If wisdom isn't automatic, then we shouldn't be relying on it. We should be relying on things we can actually check.

Now, I'll add that large language models have complicated the picture somewhat, in an interesting way. Systems trained on the vast corpus of human writing do seem to absorb something of human norms and values, more than I'd have expected. So I've updated a bit back in the other direction. But I don't think that undoes the AlphaGo Zero lesson. If anything, the worry is that as we lean harder on reinforcement learning and self-play-style optimization on top of these models, we may be moving away from that human grounding and back toward the regime where raw capability outruns any wisdom it started with.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaGo Zero was a turning point that made capability and wisdom seem separable, causing him to shift away from expecting powerful AI to become wise automatically.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss destructive cyberphysical capabilities, substantial damage, or a human-compatible AI mounting a defense.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so AlphaGo Zero was actually a pretty pivotal moment for me, and I think it's worth explaining why, because on the surface it's just a Go program.

Before 2017, I had a fairly common intuition, which was something like: in order to be really capable in a domain, you need a kind of understanding, and understanding seemed like it should come bundled with something adjacent to wisdom. The idea was that a system smart enough to be dangerous would also be smart enough to grasp the context it was operating in, what people cared about, why the goal it had been handed was the goal, and so on. Capability and good judgment felt like they'd come as a package.

What AlphaGo Zero showed me was that you can take a domain where humans had accumulated thousands of years of accumulated knowledge, strategy, aesthetics, a whole culture of play, and a system can blow past all of it with zero exposure to any of that. It never saw a human game. It just played itself, optimizing a very narrow signal, and within days it was not only superhuman, it was finding moves that human experts initially thought were mistakes and later came to see as beautiful. So it was clearly capable in the deepest sense, in that it had something like real insight into the structure of the game.

But it had absolutely nothing resembling wisdom about anything outside the game. It had no notion that Go is a game, that there are people on the other side of the board, that winning matters to anyone, or that it would be fine to lose sometimes. The capability was completely decoupled from any of the broader judgment I had implicitly assumed would come along for the ride.

And the thing that really stuck with me was the mechanism. The capability came from optimization pressure against a clean objective, in a setting where it could generate its own experience. That recipe doesn't need the world. It doesn't need human values as an input at all. So the lesson I drew was that if we get highly capable systems through something like that pathway, there's no reason to expect wisdom to show up on its own. It's not that the system would be malicious, it's that the thing we'd want, which is some robust sense of what's actually good, is just not what's being selected for.

That pushed me quite a lot toward thinking that the safety problem is real and separate from the capability problem, and it's a big part of why I've ended up focused on approaches where you try to get guarantees from the structure of the system and its specification rather than hoping that good judgment emerges as a byproduct of making things smarter.

r001.rationale: He describes AlphaGo Zero as a pivotal moment that overturned his assumption that great capability would come with wisdom, and says highly capable systems may lack broader judgment.

astra-6.text:
AlphaGo Zero helped break an intuition I had that, if you made a system sufficiently intelligent, wisdom would somehow come along with it. Here was a system that could discover strategies beyond the best human players, starting from the rules of the game and a very simple training signal. But all of that ingenuity was directed toward winning Go. There was nothing in the process that would make it step back and ask whether winning Go was a worthwhile thing to do.

And you can imagine generalizing that. A system might understand the world extremely well, including understanding human values, without having any motivation to act in accordance with those values. Understanding what we care about and caring about it are different things.

So the shift for me was to stop treating wisdom as an automatic consequence of capability. We have to account for how a system acquires its objectives, and why pursuing those objectives would actually be good for us. We can’t just assume that once it’s smart enough, it will figure out the right thing to want.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaGo Zero broke Dalrymple’s intuition that sufficient intelligence would bring wisdom, and that wisdom is not an automatic consequence of capability.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention destructive cyberphysical capabilities, substantial damage, or a human-compatible AI mounting a defense.

sol-6.1.text:
AlphaGo Zero helped me separate capability from wisdom. You have a system that can discover strategies beyond the best human players, starting from the rules and learning through self-play. But everything that makes that process successful is organized around a very narrow objective: winning at Go.

There’s no reason to expect that getting better at pursuing an objective will also make a system better at deciding whether that objective is worth pursuing. Those are different problems. And in Go, we’ve made the second problem easy by providing a clear goal in a closed environment.

So the lesson for me was that we shouldn’t expect wisdom to emerge automatically from intelligence. A system could be extraordinarily good at finding ways to achieve something while lacking the judgment we’d want about whether to do it, what consequences matter, or when to defer to people. We have to take responsibility for that distinction.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo Zero led Dalrymple to separate capability from wisdom and conclude that wisdom should not be expected to emerge automatically from intelligence.
